sections_meta.title: Comparison with the State of the Art

summaries.summary: The introduction establishes the long-standing research goal of building robotic assistants capable of performing everyday tasks through language directives, highlighting recent advancements in computer vision and natural language processing.
The Related Work section on Action Planning outlines that embodied AI tasks require multi-level reasoning that accounts for environmental dynamics, agent capabilities, and goal formulation.
This section establishes that semantic spatial maps improve search efficiency for objects, with prior works recording object positions on maps when key objects are found.

The Semantic Spatial Representation section describes earlier strategies that directly mapped visual observations and natural language instructions to sequences of low-level actions and object interaction masks.
The Approach section identifies generalization to unseen environments as a key challenge in embodied AI and notes recent proposals aim to improve generalization capabilities.
The Context-Aware Planning section explains that upon receiving a natural language command, the agent must interpret and infer task requirements such as fetching the object of interest.
Figure 3 illustrates the Context-Aware Planning (CAP) framework, which consists of a subgoal planner and detailed planners for each sub-goal to generate executable actions.
The Sub-Goal Planner generates human-interpretable sub-goals from language input, representing each sub-goal as a triplet of action, a small object, and a receptacle.
The Context Prediction section introduces three context predictors: one for the primary target object, one for a required container, and a third for additional context.
The Detailed Planners section explains that each sub-goal produced by the sub-goal planner must be rendered into agent-executable detailed actions.
The Environment-Aware Memory section addresses the challenge of perceiving 3D environments from 2D RGB images to support better navigation.
The Object Relocation Tracking section describes scenarios where the agent must relocate multiple objects of the same class to the same location.
The Object Location Caching section handles tasks requiring agents to revisit previously visited object locations to obtain objects with changed states.
The Action Policy section states that the agent must first reach target objects in close vicinity before conducting interactions, referencing approaches that plan obstacle-free paths.
The Experiments section employs the ALFRED benchmark with train, validation, and test splits for evaluating interactive instruction following performance.

The Comparison with the State of the Art section begins a quantitative analysis comparing the proposed method against prior approaches, noting comparisons with methods using only high-level representations.
